title: Musculoskeletal Pathogens
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the organisms that infect bone, joints, fascia, and muscle, and the virulence factors that let each one reach, attach to, and destroy those tissues. It moves from Staphylococcus aureus and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in bones and joints, through the setting-specific causes of osteomyelitis, to the toxin-driven destruction of gas gangrene and necrotizing fasciitis, and ends with Lyme arthritis and tuberculosis of the spine. Board questions usually give a setting (sickle cell disease, a nail through a sneaker, a dirty deep wound, a tick bite) and ask for the organism, its laboratory features, or the molecule causing the damage. If you can link each virulence factor to the lesion it produces, most of these questions answer themselves.
prerequisites: Gram stain, bacterial cell wall structure, and basic identification tests (catalase, coagulase, oxidase, hemolysis)
Bone histology and blood supply, including the metaphysis and growth plate (MS-2)
Antigen presentation by MHC class II to CD4 T cells and Th1 granuloma formation (IM-5)
Limb muscle compartments and the attachments of psoas major (MS-5)

connections.how: Reactive arthritis and antibiotic-refractory Lyme arthritis show joint inflammation that continues after, or without, live organisms in the joint.
This chapter supplies the organisms and mechanisms behind the clinical patterns of osteomyelitis, septic arthritis, and myonecrosis taught there.
Terminal complement deficiency explains recurrent disseminated Neisseria infection, and M protein and protein A show two different ways bacteria defeat opsonization.
Borrelia burgdorferi and Streptococcus pyogenes also injure the heart, through Lyme carditis with AV block and rheumatic fever.
Sickle cell disease predisposes to Salmonella osteomyelitis through bone infarcts and functional asplenia, and clostridial alpha toxin causes intravascular hemolysis.

terms.def: Infection of bone and marrow, reaching bone through the blood, from a contiguous focus, or by direct inoculation.
Infection of a joint space, usually by bacteria, producing purulent synovial fluid that can destroy cartilage within days.
A fragment of dead bone left within an infected area after its blood supply is lost.
A shell of new reactive bone laid down by periosteum that has been lifted off by pus.
A bacterial surface molecule that binds a specific host molecule, such as collagen or fibronectin, so the organism can attach to tissue.
A community of bacteria embedded in a self-made polysaccharide matrix on a surface, protected from antibodies, phagocytes, and many antibiotics.
Change in the structure of a surface antigen through gene recombination, so antibodies made against the old form no longer bind.
A phospholipase C that hydrolyzes lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) in cell membranes; the alpha toxin of Clostridium perfringens.
A toxin that binds MHC class II and the T cell receptor beta chain outside the peptide groove, activating a large fraction of T cells at once.
Death of skeletal muscle, the defining lesion of clostridial gas gangrene.
Tuberculosis of the spine, with destruction and collapse of vertebral bodies.
A collection of caseous material without the heat and redness of an acute pyogenic abscess, typical of tuberculosis.

sections.title: Staphylococcus aureus in bone and joint infection

blocks.text: Staphylococcus aureus is a gram-positive coccus that grows in grapelike clusters. It is catalase positive, which separates staphylococci from streptococci, and coagulase positive, which separates it from coagulase-negative species such as S. epidermidis. Free coagulase activates prothrombin so that fibrinogen is converted to fibrin, and bound clumping factor coats the organism in fibrinogen, so the bacteria hide inside a fibrin shell. About a third of people carry S. aureus in the anterior nares, which gives it frequent access to the blood through minor skin breaks.
Why it is the leading bone and joint pathogen

Its success rests on three abilities. First, surface adhesins anchored in the cell wall (often called MSCRAMMs, microbial surface components recognizing adhesive matrix molecules) bind collagen, fibronectin, and fibrinogen, which are exposed in bone matrix, cartilage, and synovium. Second, protein A binds the Fc region of IgG. The antibody is then held backward, with its Fc pointing at the bacterium instead of outward, so neutrophil Fc receptors cannot grab it and opsonization fails. Third, on dead bone and implanted hardware the organisms form a biofilm, a polysaccharide matrix in which slow-growing bacteria are shielded from antibodies, phagocytes, and many antibiotics. This is why infection on a device or a sequestrum tends to persist until the foreign material or dead bone is removed.

blocks.title: Staphylococcus aureus virulence factors and their effects in bone and joint
rows: Bind matrix proteins in bone, cartilage, synovium
Binds IgG by its Fc region
Convert or bind fibrinogen to fibrin
Fibrin coat hides bacteria; walls off abscesses
Polysaccharide matrix on dead bone or hardware
blocks.caption: Each factor maps to a step: attachment, escape from opsonization, protection, and tissue damage.

blocks.text: In children, hematogenous osteomyelitis favors the metaphysis of long bones. Capillary loops beneath the growth plate turn into wide venous sinusoids where flow is slow and phagocytes are sparse, so circulating bacteria settle there. In infants younger than about 18 months, vessels still cross the growth plate, so infection can reach the epiphysis and joint. Where the metaphysis lies inside the joint capsule (hip and shoulder), osteomyelitis can rupture into the joint. In adults, hematogenous infection more often involves the vertebrae. S. aureus is also the most common cause of septic arthritis overall, which produces turbid synovial fluid, often above 50,000 cells per microliter, mostly neutrophils, whose proteases destroy cartilage within days.

blocks.title: Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis in a child
steps: Transient S. aureus bacteremia
Bacteria lodge in slow metaphyseal sinusoids and bind matrix
Neutrophils and bacterial enzymes form pus
Rising pressure and thrombosis cut blood supply
Dead bone remains as a sequestrum
Pus lifts periosteum, which forms an involucrum
blocks.caption: From seeding to the chronic lesion; the sequestrum then harbors biofilm that resists clearance.

blocks.predict: Predict whether an S. aureus strain lacking protein A would be cleared more easily from the blood of an immunized host.
blocks.explain: Without protein A, opsonizing IgG binds by its Fab region with the Fc facing outward, so neutrophil Fc receptors can engage it and phagocytosis proceeds.

sections.title: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and disseminated gonococcal infection

blocks.text: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus, the paired cocci having flattened adjacent sides, and in urethral or joint exudate it is often seen inside neutrophils. It is oxidase positive and ferments glucose but not maltose, which separates it from N. meningitidis (glucose and maltose). It is fastidious, growing best on chocolate agar or selective Thayer-Martin medium in increased CO2, and it has no polysaccharide capsule.
Virulence: attachment and escape from adaptive immunity

Type IV pili attach the organism to nonciliated columnar epithelium of the urethra, cervix, rectum, and pharynx and resist flushing by urine. The pilin gene is expressed from one locus while many silent partial copies sit elsewhere in the genome, and recombination of a silent copy into the expression locus changes the pilus antigen. Opacity (Opa) proteins switch on and off by phase variation. Because antibodies against one variant miss the next, infection gives no lasting immunity, reinfection is common, and no vaccine exists. IgA1 protease cleaves secretory IgA1 in its hinge region, removing the main antibody defense of mucosa. Lipooligosaccharide (a short-chain endotoxin) drives inflammation, and sialylation of it helps resist complement.

Killing of Neisseria depends heavily on the membrane attack complex. People with deficiency of terminal complement components (C5 to C9) therefore get recurrent disseminated Neisseria infection. Dissemination is also more common in women, especially during menstruation and pregnancy, when cervical conditions favor bacteremia.

blocks.title: Two presentations of disseminated gonococcal infection
rows: Bacteremia seeds tendon sheaths, skin, and joints, possibly with immune complexes
Organisms settle and multiply in one joint
Migratory polyarthralgia; tenosynovitis of wrists, hands, ankles
Monoarthritis or oligoarthritis, often knee, wrist, or ankle
Few painless pustules on a red base, on the extremities
Blood sometimes positive; joint fluid usually negative
Synovial fluid culture positive in about half or fewer
blocks.caption: The two forms often overlap in time; the first can evolve into the second.

blocks.text: The typical patient is a sexually active young adult, often with an asymptomatic genital infection, who develops fever, tender swollen tendon sheaths over the wrist or hand, and scattered pustules. Because the joint culture is often negative, the diagnosis rests on finding the organism at mucosal sites (urethra, cervix, rectum, pharynx) by culture or nucleic acid amplification, or in blood. In this age group gonococcus is a leading cause of acute septic arthritis, while S. aureus remains the most common cause across all ages.

S. aureus is the most likely cause of osteomyelitis in almost every setting, so board questions test the exceptions. Each exception follows from how the organism reaches bone or why host defenses fail in that setting, and remembering the reason is more reliable than memorizing a list.

rows: Salmonella (nontyphoidal): gram-negative rod, non-lactose fermenter, H2S producer
Bone infarcts give dead tissue to seed; functional asplenia impairs clearance; gut microinfarcts let bacteria enter blood
Contaminated water and equipment; vertebrae and sternoclavicular joint typical
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: gram-negative rod, oxidase positive, non-lactose fermenter, blue-green pigment
Moist foam insole harbors the organism; puncture inoculates calcaneus or metatarsal
Oral flora of cats and dogs; sharp cat teeth inoculate periosteum; cellulitis within about a day
Staphylococcus epidermidis: gram-positive clusters, coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive
Skin flora introduced at surgery; biofilm on foreign material; indolent course
Vertebrae with slow course and constitutional symptoms
Hematogenous seeding of vascular vertebral bodies (Pott disease)
blocks.caption: The setting predicts the organism because it determines the route of entry or the host defect.

blocks.text: Sickle cell disease shows how host defects shape the organism. Repeated splenic infarction leaves the patient functionally asplenic, which impairs clearance of encapsulated and opsonized bacteria from the blood. Vaso-occlusion in bowel wall lets enteric organisms such as Salmonella enter the circulation, and infarcted marrow and bone give them a poorly perfused, devitalized place to grow. Infection is often in the diaphysis and can be multifocal. Salmonella is the classic association and in many series the most frequent cause in these patients, but S. aureus still causes a large share. Bone infarction during a pain crisis can look very much like osteomyelitis, which is a common diagnostic problem.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an obligate aerobe that thrives in moist environments, so it lives in the wet foam of an athletic shoe and is driven into the foot when a nail passes through the sole. Its grapelike odor and pyocyanin pigment help identify it in culture. Pasteurella multocida is part of normal oral flora in cats and dogs; infection begins as rapidly spreading cellulitis within about 24 hours of the bite, and cat bites, being deep punctures, more often reach bone or tendon sheath.

Staphylococcus epidermidis is a low-virulence skin organism that becomes a pathogen when foreign material is present. It adheres to plastic and metal and builds a polysaccharide biofilm, so prosthetic joint infections it causes are often low grade, appear months after surgery, and present with pain and loosening rather than high fever. Contiguous spread from a foot ulcer in diabetes, by contrast, is usually polymicrobial.

blocks.title: Worked example: reasoning from the setting
blocks.text: A 9-year-old with sickle cell disease has fever and a tender, swollen thigh. Start with what is broken in this host. Functional asplenia weakens clearance of bacteria from the blood, gut microinfarcts let enteric gram-negative rods reach the circulation, and infarcted bone gives them dead tissue to colonize. That chain points to Salmonella, a gram-negative, non-lactose-fermenting rod that produces H2S. S. aureus remains possible, because it is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in general. Bone infarction from a pain crisis can mimic infection, so a culture of blood or bone, not imaging alone, separates infarct from osteomyelitis and identifies the organism.

Clostridium perfringens is a large, gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming rod. Its spores survive for years in soil and in the intestinal tract of humans and animals, so wounds contaminated with soil or feces receive them. Unlike most clostridia it is nonmotile, and spores are seldom seen in clinical specimens. On blood agar it gives a double zone of hemolysis: an inner zone of complete hemolysis from theta toxin and an outer zone of partial hemolysis from alpha toxin. On a Gram stain of wound fluid it appears as broad, boxcar-shaped rods with strikingly few neutrophils.
Alpha toxin and myonecrosis

Germination needs a low oxidation-reduction potential. That exists in deep wounds with crushed or devitalized muscle, retained foreign material, or impaired blood supply, as in battlefield injury, open fractures, or compartment injury. Once growing, the organism secretes alpha toxin, a phospholipase C (lecithinase) that hydrolyzes phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) and sphingomyelin in the outer leaflet of plasma membranes. Muscle fibers, red cells, platelets, and endothelium lose membrane integrity and die. At lower concentrations the toxin activates platelets and leukocytes inside vessels, forming aggregates that occlude small vessels and hold neutrophils back from the tissue, which is why the lesion has so little inflammation. Theta toxin (perfringolysin O), a cholesterol-dependent pore-forming toxin, adds to the damage.

Dead, ischemic muscle widens the anaerobic zone, so the infection advances along muscle bundles at a rate measured in hours. Fermentation of tissue sugars releases hydrogen and carbon dioxide, which produce crepitus on palpation and gas in tissue planes on imaging. Spreading hemolysis causes hemoglobinuria and jaundice, and released toxin and tissue breakdown products cause shock and renal failure. The skin over the lesion turns pale, then bronze, with hemorrhagic bullae and a thin, foul, brownish discharge, and pain is severe and out of proportion to the visible wound.

blocks.title: Gas gangrene
steps: Deep contaminated wound with devitalized, poorly perfused muscle
Spores germinate in the low-oxygen tissue
Alpha toxin hydrolyzes membrane lecithin
Muscle, red cells, and endothelium die
Necrosis enlarges the anaerobic zone; spread accelerates
Fermentation gas gives crepitus; hemolysis and shock follow
blocks.caption: Tissue destruction creates the conditions for further growth, so spread is self-reinforcing.

blocks.text: Two distinctions are commonly tested. C. perfringens food poisoning is a different disease, caused by an enterotoxin released when large numbers of vegetative cells, ingested in slowly cooled or reheated meat, sporulate in the gut, and it causes self-limited watery diarrhea. Spontaneous (nontraumatic) gas gangrene without a wound suggests Clostridium septicum, which is associated with colon cancer and neutropenia because organisms enter the blood through damaged bowel mucosa.

blocks.predict: Predict the Gram stain of fluid from a crepitant, rapidly spreading thigh wound in gas gangrene: many neutrophils or few?
blocks.explain: Few. Alpha toxin lyses neutrophils that arrive and, at lower concentrations, makes platelets and leukocytes aggregate in vessels, so neutrophils do not reach the tissue in normal numbers.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on alpha toxin and myonecrosis.

sections.title: Streptococcus pyogenes, necrotizing fasciitis, and toxic shock

blocks.text: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A streptococcus) is a gram-positive coccus in chains. It is catalase negative, beta-hemolytic (complete hemolysis from streptolysins O and S), sensitive to bacitracin, and PYR positive. Its hyaluronic acid capsule resembles host connective tissue and is poorly immunogenic, which adds to its ability to evade phagocytes.
Resisting phagocytosis and spreading through tissue

M protein is a coiled-coil fibrillar protein that projects from the surface. It binds host complement regulators such as factor H and C4b-binding protein and binds fibrinogen, so C3b deposition is limited and the bacterium is not opsonized. Antibody against the specific M type restores phagocytosis, which is why immunity is type specific and repeated infections occur. Hyaluronidase digests hyaluronic acid in connective tissue ground substance, streptokinase converts plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve fibrin that would wall off infection, and DNases thin pus by cleaving DNA from dead neutrophils. Together these let infection travel along the superficial fascia, the plane between subcutaneous fat and deep muscle fascia.

In necrotizing fasciitis this spread outpaces the skin findings. Bacteria and toxins thrombose the small perforating vessels that pass through the fascia to the skin, so the skin first looks only mildly red while pain is severe and out of proportion. Later the skin becomes dusky and blistered and then numb as cutaneous nerves die. Group A streptococcus alone causes monomicrobial (type II) disease, whereas type I disease is polymicrobial, with anaerobes, and more often has gas.
Superantigens and toxic shock

Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (for example SpeA and SpeC) are superantigens. A conventional antigen is processed into a peptide that sits in the groove of an MHC class II molecule and activates only the rare T cells whose receptors fit it, a tiny fraction of all T cells. A superantigen is not processed; it clamps the outside of MHC class II to the variable region of the T cell receptor beta chain, activating every T cell with that beta chain family, up to about 20 percent of all T cells. The resulting cytokine flood produces shock.

blocks.title: How a superantigen causes toxic shock
steps: Pyrogenic exotoxin released from infected tissue
Toxin binds MHC class II outside the peptide groove
Same toxin binds T cell receptor beta chain
Up to about 20 percent of T cells activate
Massive IL-2, TNF, IFN-gamma, and IL-1 release
Fever, capillary leak, hypotension, multiorgan failure
blocks.caption: Bypassing antigen processing converts a local infection into a systemic cytokine storm.

blocks.title: Streptococcal and staphylococcal toxic shock compared
rows: Deep soft tissue infection such as necrotizing fasciitis
Tampon, nasal packing, wound with colonization
blocks.caption: Both are superantigen diseases; the streptococcal form usually has an invasive tissue focus.

blocks.text: Borrelia burgdorferi is a spirochete, a long, thin, helical bacterium that moves by periplasmic flagella lying between the inner and outer membranes. It stains poorly with the Gram stain, grows slowly in special liquid medium, and is rarely cultured in practice. In the United States it is carried by Ixodes scapularis (the black-legged or deer tick) in the Northeast, mid-Atlantic, and upper Midwest, and by Ixodes pacificus on the Pacific coast.
The transmission cycle

Borrelia is rarely passed through tick eggs, so larvae hatch uninfected. They acquire the organism during their single blood meal on an infected white-footed mouse, the main reservoir, and keep it when they molt into nymphs. Nymphs feed the following late spring and summer; they are about the size of a poppy seed, often go unnoticed, and are the stage that transmits most human infections. Adult ticks feed and mate on white-tailed deer. Deer sustain the tick population but are not a competent reservoir for the bacterium.

blocks.title: Ixodes life cycle and Borrelia transmission
steps: Eggs hatch into uninfected larvae
Larvae feed on infected white-footed mice
Infected larvae molt into nymphs
Nymphs feed on mice or humans, transmitting Borrelia
Nymphs molt into adults that feed on deer
Adult females lay eggs
blocks.caption: About two years; mice infect larvae, nymphs infect people, and deer feed adults.

blocks.text: Transmission is delayed because the spirochetes start in the tick midgut, where they express outer surface protein A (OspA) to bind the gut wall. The blood meal triggers multiplication and a switch to OspC, and the organisms migrate to the salivary glands before entering the skin. For this reason risk is low if the tick is removed within about 36 hours of attachment. In the skin the organisms spread outward, producing the expanding erythema migrans rash, then disseminate through the blood to joints, heart, and nervous system. Antigenic variation of the surface lipoprotein VlsE helps them persist.

blocks.title: Stages of Lyme disease
rows: Multiple erythema migrans, facial nerve palsy (can be bilateral), lymphocytic meningitis, carditis with AV block, migratory joint pain
Intermittent or persistent arthritis of one or a few large joints, especially the knee
blocks.caption: Untreated patients may skip stages; late arthritis can be the first recognized sign.

blocks.text: Late Lyme arthritis follows invasion of the synovium. Spirochetal lipoproteins activate Toll-like receptor 2 on synovial cells and macrophages, and the adaptive response adds T cells and antibody, giving synovial hypertrophy and attacks of large effusions that are often less painful than their size suggests. Synovial fluid is inflammatory, commonly about 10,000 to 25,000 cells per microliter with neutrophil predominance. Spirochete DNA can be detected in joint fluid by PCR, and patients have high IgG antibody levels. In a minority, inflammation persists after the organism is eliminated (antibiotic-refractory Lyme arthritis), linked to certain HLA-DR alleles and to autoimmune responses in the synovium.

blocks.title: Worked example: timing of transmission
blocks.text: A hiker in Connecticut removes an engorged nymphal tick and estimates it had been attached for 2 days. Reason through the tick first. Spirochetes sit in the midgut bound by OspA and must multiply, switch to OspC, and migrate to the salivary glands after feeding starts, a process that takes about 36 hours or more. Engorgement shows feeding long enough for that migration, so the risk of transmission is real. A flat nymph removed within a day carries a much lower risk. If the bacterium was transmitted, expect an expanding erythema migrans lesion within about 3 to 30 days, and, without treatment, possible arthritis of the knee months later.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slow-growing, obligately aerobic rod whose cell wall is rich in mycolic acids. These long-chain lipids resist decolorization by acid alcohol (acid fast on Ziehl-Neelsen stain) and protect the organism inside macrophages. Sulfatides help block phagosome-lysosome fusion, and cord factor (trehalose dimycolate) stimulates TNF release and granuloma formation. The spine is the most common site of skeletal tuberculosis, accounting for about half of cases.
Hematogenous seeding and granuloma formation

During primary pulmonary infection, bacilli carried by macrophages enter lymph and blood and seed distant organs before cell-mediated immunity develops. The vertebral bodies are favored because they hold red marrow with a rich arterial supply, and the valveless paravertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus) offers a second route. The lower thoracic and upper lumbar spine are most often affected. The seeded focus may stay latent for years and reactivate when immunity wanes, and the chest radiograph often shows no active lung disease by then.

Dendritic cells present mycobacterial antigens to CD4 T cells, and IL-12 drives a Th1 response. Interferon-gamma activates macrophages, which become epithelioid cells and fuse into Langhans giant cells, and TNF holds the granuloma together. The center undergoes caseous necrosis, a cheesy, structureless necrosis that destroys the trabecular bone.

blocks.title: From seeding to deformity in Pott disease
steps: Bacilli seed the anterior vertebral body near the endplate
Caseating granulomas destroy trabecular bone
Infection spreads beneath the anterior longitudinal ligament and across the disc
Adjacent vertebrae and disc space collapse
Anterior wedge collapse with intact posterior elements gives a gibbus
Caseous material tracks down the psoas sheath
blocks.caption: Destruction centers on the anterior column, so the spine angles forward.

blocks.text: Because the posterior elements usually survive, the collapsing anterior column tips the spine forward into a sharp angular kyphosis, the gibbus deformity. Retropulsed bone, granulation tissue, or abscess can compress the spinal cord and cause paraparesis (Pott paraplegia). The abscess is a cold abscess, lacking the heat and redness of pyogenic pus. The psoas major arises from the lumbar vertebral bodies and discs (T12 to L5), so caseous material from the lower thoracic and lumbar spine can track down its sheath, presenting as a groin mass or pain on hip extension.

blocks.title: Tuberculous versus pyogenic vertebral infection
rows: Months; night sweats, weight loss, low fever
Days to weeks; often high fever
Several contiguous levels, skip lesions possible
Usually one disc and the two adjacent vertebrae
Large, calcified, cold, may track along psoas
Biopsy: caseating granulomas, acid-fast bacilli, culture or PCR
blocks.caption: The slow course and anterior spread under the longitudinal ligament distinguish tuberculous spondylitis.

blocks.predict: Why does vertebral tuberculosis produce a sharp angular kyphosis rather than a smooth curve?
blocks.explain: Destruction is concentrated in the anterior bodies of a few adjacent vertebrae while the posterior elements remain, so the spine hinges forward at one short segment.

integration.text: Anatomy and physiology explain where these organisms settle. Slow flow in metaphyseal sinusoids, the rich arterial and venous supply of vertebral bodies, infarcted bone in sickle cell disease, and the fascial planes of the limbs each create a site where a particular organism can grow. Immunology explains why some hosts fail: protein A and M protein defeat opsonization by different routes, terminal complement deficiency allows disseminated Neisseria, functional asplenia allows Salmonella, and the Th1 granuloma both contains and destroys tissue in tuberculosis.

Pathology follows the virulence factor. Enzymes and toxins (lecithinase, hyaluronidase, streptokinase) cause rapid, spreading necrosis; superantigens cause shock through T cell activation rather than direct tissue damage; and biofilm and granulomas cause chronic infection that persists around dead bone or implants. The settings in this chapter are probabilities, not rules. S. aureus remains common in nearly every group, cultures can be negative in gonococcal and Lyme arthritis, and sterile inflammation, as in bone infarction or antibiotic-refractory Lyme arthritis, can mimic infection.

summary: S. aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis and septic arthritis because matrix adhesins attach it to bone, protein A binds IgG Fc to block opsonization, and biofilm protects it on dead bone and hardware.
In children, hematogenous osteomyelitis seeds the slow-flowing metaphyseal sinusoids, leading to sequestrum and involucrum.

N. gonorrhoeae evades immunity by pilus antigenic variation and IgA1 protease; terminal complement deficiency predisposes to disseminated infection with tenosynovitis, pustules, and polyarthralgia or purulent monoarthritis.

Settings predict exceptions to S. aureus: Salmonella in sickle cell disease, Pseudomonas after a sneaker puncture or injection drug use, Pasteurella after animal bites, S. epidermidis on prostheses, and M. tuberculosis in the spine.
C. perfringens alpha toxin is a lecithinase that destroys cell membranes, causing myonecrosis, hemolysis, and gas gangrene with few neutrophils.
S. pyogenes M protein blocks complement opsonization; hyaluronidase and streptokinase let infection spread along fascia; pyrogenic exotoxins are superantigens that cause toxic shock.
Ixodes larvae acquire Borrelia from white-footed mice, nymphs transmit it to people after about 36 hours or more of attachment, and deer feed adult ticks.
Late Lyme arthritis is an intermittent large-joint arthritis, most often of the knee, months after infection.
Pott disease is hematogenous tuberculosis of the anterior vertebral bodies, with caseating granulomas, collapse into a gibbus, and cold psoas abscess.

verify: Whether Salmonella or S. aureus is the most common cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease differs between series; the notes present Salmonella as the classic association with S. aureus still common. Confirm the answer NABNE expects.
The attachment time for Borrelia transmission is given as about 36 hours in the competency; some sources give 36 to 48 hours or more.

Figures quoted as approximations: about half of skeletal tuberculosis in the spine, about 20 percent of T cells activated by a superantigen, Lyme synovial fluid counts of about 10,000 to 25,000 cells per microliter, septic synovial fluid often above 50,000 cells per microliter, and gonococcal synovial cultures positive in about half of purulent arthritis.
The role of immune complexes in the arthritis-dermatitis form of disseminated gonococcal infection is not settled; it is presented as a contributing mechanism.

Confirm whether NABNE expects names such as MSCRAMM, OspA and OspC, VlsE, SpeA and SpeC, Batson plexus, and type I versus type II necrotizing fasciitis, or only the virulence factors named in the competencies.
